items.title: Ann Rabson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 21, 2007
items.q: My sister went to the New England Conservatory of Music. And now she’s teaching at Berklee.

ctx.x: Well I can tell you that schooled musicians are often times envious of that ability to play things that maybe you don’t know what they are but you know they sound good. Because it happened to me, getting out of college and feeling like I knew everything and then getting in with groups that were basically self-taught musicians and seeing the way they operated and being envious of that and the hearing that they had developed.

But you know you can develop both. Because you’ve obviously got both. My sister went to the New England Conservatory of Music. And now she’s teaching at Berklee. And she is one of the most passionate improvisational musicians. I know she doesn’t process things through her head. I really know, which to me is the absolute only way I can work. And the way I want to work is just to not to think. People say what do you think about when you’re playing. And I think, I say, hopefully nothing. Because you’ve just got to…

Yeah, it’s a tough question to really answer: what do you really think about when you’re playing. But you know, in sitting next to you the last couple of nights and I’m watching you, when you come down on that piano you sort of know what you’re going to hit first and then you see what happens.
